How to save money

In shooting, the biggest saving usually comes from a sensible plan, not from cheap gear. Here are some common ways to spend less. One thing stays fixed: do not save on safety. Safety glasses, hearing protection and a gun in good working order come first.

Club membership. In many clubs, members pay less for targets and training, can enter club shoots and may get discounts on cartridges. If you shoot regularly, membership often pays for itself. Compare several clubs.

Cartridges in bulk. Buying cartridges in large batches is usually cheaper than buying single boxes. Do it only where the law lets you buy and store that quantity, and keep them dry and cool as your country's rules require. Club members often buy together. Storage: Choosing, storing and transporting cartridges.

Mind the competition rules. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting competitions, reloaded cartridges (used cases filled again, often at home) are not allowed, and a cartridge may hold at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated). The rules: Chapter 7 · Cartridge rules, Chapter 18 · Prohibited ammunition. So home-loaded cartridges do not help at competitions. For training, many shooters use lighter factory cartridges that kick less (low-recoil cartridges); ask your coach which load suits you.

Used gear. Besides the gun, vests, cases and chokes (screw-in tubes at the muzzle that set how widely the shot spreads) are often bought used. Buy used chokes only if they fit your gun's choke system, are undamaged and suit the shot you use, for example steel; if in doubt, ask a gunsmith (Fixed and interchangeable chokes). But replace safety glasses with scratched or cracked lenses: they may no longer protect as they should. Earplugs are personal, so get your own.

Train with a purpose. A few rounds with a clear task from your coach give more than many cartridges fired just because. Where the law of your country allows it, dry mounting costs nothing: you practise the gun mount at home, without cartridges, with a gun you have checked is unloaded. Do it the way your coach showed you (Dry practice of the mount). A training diary helps you see what works.

Shared trips. Travelling to competitions together and sharing travel and accommodation saves money. ClayArena is also preparing ClayAway: organised training tours that will bundle coaching, accommodation and transfers into one package.

Key points

  • Do not save on safety.
  • Club membership often pays for itself.
  • Buy cartridges in bulk only where the law allows buying and storing them.
  • Reloaded cartridges are not allowed in FITASC competitions.
  • Train with a purpose, dry mount where the law allows, share trips.

Did you know?

Many clubs have club guns that members can use in training, so you can take your time before buying your own.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What should you not save on?

    1. The brand and colour of your vest
    2. Eye and ear protection, a gun in good order
    3. How many club shoots you enter
    Answer

    Eye and ear protection, a gun in good order

    Safety comes first: protection for eyes and ears and a gun in good order.

  2. May you use reloaded cartridges at FITASC competitions?

    1. Yes, if they are good quality
    2. Yes, but only in Compak® Sporting
    3. No, both rulebooks forbid them
    Answer

    No, both rulebooks forbid them

    The rules of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting both forbid reloaded cartridges.

  3. When does it make sense to buy cartridges in bulk?

    1. Where the law allows buying and storing it
    2. Anywhere, since bulk is cheaper
    3. Only in the week before a championship
    Answer

    Where the law allows buying and storing it

    Rules on buying and storing cartridges differ between countries.
